n: Pentecost arrives — fifty days after Passover — and the believers are gathered together in one place, united in heart.

f.g: Greek for “fiftieth.” Also called the Feast of Weeks, a harvest festival; Jewish tradition later linked it to the giving of the law at Sinai.

n: Suddenly a sound like a roaring wind fills the house. In both Hebrew and Greek, the same word can mean wind, breath, and spirit.
Flames like divided tongues of fire appear and rest on each of them. Fire symbolizes God’s presence and the purifying power of the Spirit.

f.w: cloven tongues like as of fire
f.g: cloven = divided, split.

n: All are filled with the Holy Ghost and begin speaking in other languages as the Spirit enables them. The promised baptism of the Spirit has come.
Jerusalem is crowded with devout Jews from all over the world who had come for the festival or settled in the city.

f.w: out of every nation under heaven
f.g: Jews of the Diaspora, scattered across the Roman and Parthian empires.

n: Hearing the commotion, a crowd gathers and is bewildered: each one hears the disciples speaking in his own native language.

f.g: noised abroad = reported widely.
The same verb is used in the Greek Old Testament for the confusion at Babel; Pentecost reverses Babel.

n: Amazed, they ask whether these speakers aren’t all Galileans — unschooled country folk with a recognizable accent.

f.g: Galileans had a distinctive accent.

n: How can each of them hear their own mother tongue?

f.g: Their native language, learned from birth.

n: Luke lists the peoples present, moving roughly from east to west: Parthians, Medes, Elamites (modern Iran), Mesopotamia (Iraq), Judea, and regions of Asia Minor (Turkey).

f.g: Descendants of Jews exiled east centuries earlier by Assyria and Babylon.
Here the Roman province in western Asia Minor, not the continent.

n: The list continues across Asia Minor, North Africa, and even Rome — both Jews by birth and proselytes, Gentiles who had converted to Judaism.

f.g: A city in modern Libya.
proselytes = converts to Judaism.
Visitors from Rome.

n: Cretans and Arabs complete the list. All hear the disciples declaring God’s mighty works in their own languages. The gospel is for every nation.

f.g: People of the island of Crete.

n: Everyone is astonished and perplexed, asking what it means.

f.g: were in doubt = were perplexed, at a loss.

n: Others sneer that the disciples are simply drunk.

f.g: Sweet new wine — a mocking dismissal.

n: Peter stands with the other eleven apostles and boldly addresses the crowd — the same Peter who denied Jesus weeks earlier, now transformed by the Holy Ghost.

f.w: Peter, standing up with the eleven

f.g: hearken = listen carefully.

n: These men aren’t drunk, he says with a touch of humor — it’s only nine in the morning.

f.w: the third hour of the day
f.g: About 9 a.m., the hour of morning prayer and sacrifice.

n: Instead, this is what the prophet Joel foretold.

f.g: When Moroni appeared to Joseph Smith, he quoted this same passage from Joel and said it was not yet fulfilled but soon would be.

n: Peter quotes Joel: in the last days God will pour out his Spirit on all people. Sons and daughters will prophesy, young men see visions, old men dream dreams — the Spirit is not limited by age or gender.

f.w: I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh
your sons and your daughters shall prophesy

n: Even servants and handmaids — the lowest in society — will receive the Spirit and prophesy.

f.g: handmaidens = female servants.

n: Joel’s prophecy continues with signs in the heavens and on earth: blood, fire, and smoke — imagery of God’s coming judgment.
The sun will darken and the moon turn to blood before the great day of the Lord. Peter sees the last days as having begun, with fuller fulfillment still ahead.

f.w: The sun shall be turned into darkness

f.g: notable = glorious, conspicuous.

n: And everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. Peter is about to show that “the Lord” is Jesus.

f.w: whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be saved

n: Peter now turns to Jesus of Nazareth: God endorsed him publicly through miracles, wonders, and signs that they themselves witnessed.

f.g: approved = attested, shown to be genuine.

n: Jesus was handed over according to God’s set plan and foreknowledge — yet they are still responsible for crucifying him through lawless hands. God’s plan doesn’t erase human accountability.

f.w: the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God

f.g: Literally “lawless hands” — likely the Romans, who did not have God’s law.

n: But God raised him up, freeing him from death’s agony, because death could not possibly keep its hold on him.

f.g: holden = held.

n: Peter cites David in Psalm 16: “I saw the Lord always before me; he is at my right hand so I will not be shaken.”
So the psalmist’s heart rejoices and his body rests in hope.

f.w: my flesh shall rest in hope

n: God will not abandon his soul to the realm of the dead nor let his Holy One see decay. “Hell” here means the world of spirits, not the place of punishment.

f.g: Greek hadēs, Hebrew sheol — the abode of the dead.
corruption = bodily decay.

n: God has shown him the paths of life and will fill him with joy in his presence.

f.g: countenance = face, presence.

n: Peter argues plainly: David died, was buried, and his tomb is still in Jerusalem. So he wasn’t speaking of himself.

f.w: his sepulchre is with us unto this day

n: David was a prophet who knew God had sworn an oath to put one of his descendants on his throne — the Messiah.

f.w: God had sworn with an oath to him

n: Foreseeing this, David spoke of the Messiah’s resurrection: not left among the dead, his body not decaying.
God raised this Jesus — and all the apostles are eyewitnesses. This is the heart of their testimony.
Exalted to God’s right hand, Jesus received the promised Holy Ghost from the Father and has poured out what they now see and hear.

f.w: by the right hand of God exalted

f.g: shed forth = poured out.

n: David did not ascend to heaven, yet he wrote in Psalm 110: “The LORD said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand.”

f.w: The LORD said unto my Lord
f.g: “LORD” in capitals stands for the divine name; Peter applies “my Lord” to the exalted Christ.

n: …until God makes his enemies a footstool for his feet — a picture of total victory.

f.g: Conquerors sometimes placed their feet on defeated enemies’ necks.

n: Peter’s conclusion: all Israel should know for certain that God has made this Jesus — whom they crucified — both Lord and Messiah.
Cut to the heart, the listeners ask the apostles, “Brothers, what should we do?” Real conviction leads to a desire to change.

Peter answers clearly: repent, be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and receive the gift of the Holy Ghost. These are the first principles and ordinances of the gospel.

f.w: Repent, and be baptized every one of you
f.r: Articles of Faith 1:4; 3 Nephi 27:20; 2 Nephi 31:17; D&C 49:13-14

f.g: remission = forgiveness, cancellation of a debt.

n: The promise is for them, their children, and those far away — everyone the Lord calls. It reaches across generations and nations.

f.w: to all that are afar off

n: With many more words Peter testifies and urges them to save themselves from this crooked generation.

f.g: untoward = crooked, perverse.

n: Those who gladly accept his message are baptized — about three thousand that day. At Sinai, tradition recalls, three thousand died (Exodus 32:28); at Pentecost, three thousand receive new life.
The new converts devote themselves to four things: the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, breaking bread together (likely including the sacrament), and prayer.
A sense of awe settles on everyone as the apostles perform many wonders and signs.

f.g: Here reverent awe, not terror.

n: The believers stay together and share everything they own.
They sell property and possessions and distribute to anyone in need — an early form of the law of consecration.
Every day they worship together at the temple and share meals in homes with glad, sincere hearts. Early Christians still saw themselves as faithful Jews.

f.g: Simplicity, sincerity, undivided devotion.
Or “at home” — in private homes, the first Christian meeting places.

n: Praising God and respected by the people, they see the Lord add new believers every day. Growth is credited to the Lord, not to clever methods.

f.w: the Lord added to the church daily
